title: Speaking truth
hookLine: the best struggle is a word of truth before an unjust ruler: out loud, or in private?
tomorrow: why would the Prophet hold up two fingers?

lines: THE CALL-OUT, OR THE QUIET TALK?
A WORD OF TRUTH BEFORE POWER.
cards: A call-out video racks up views. A quiet talk in someone's office gets none. Online, out loud can look like the only brave option.
Is it? The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ named a kind of courage that sounds like it settles the question: the best struggle is a word of truth before an unjust ruler. Said to the face of power.
But even inside the tradition, people have argued about which room that word belongs in.

teach.b: The hadith is in Sunan Abu Dawud: the best jihad, the best struggle, is a word of justice before an unjust ruler. Other reports say a word of truth. Not a sword.
A sentence, said when it costs something.

Sahih Muslim adds a ladder: whoever sees a wrong, let him change it with his hand; if he can't, with his tongue; if he can't, with his heart, and that is the weakest of faith. So the speaking is settled.

One view: say it openly. The word in the hadith is spoken before the ruler, where it counts, and a wrong done in public can need a public answer. The other view, which some scholars press: begin in private.

They point to a report in Musnad Ahmad: whoever wants to advise a person in authority should take him by the hand and do it alone; if he listens, good, and if not, you've done your part. Each at its best?
Open speech protects the people being harmed, who need to hear someone say it. Private speech protects the dignity of the one corrected and gives him room to change.
And both sides agree on one thing: silence about a real wrong isn't the safe middle.
The word gets said. The argument is about the room.

how: Muslims draw on this hadith and the hand-tongue-heart hadith when deciding whether to speak up about a wrong; scholars and communities differ on when correction should be public and when private.

o: speaking only in words taken from scripture
saying what's right, even when it costs you
never telling a lie, even a polite one

games.q: who says what about speaking up — tap the pairs.
p: a word of justice before an unjust ruler
change it with hand, tongue or heart
changing it only in the heart

s: in Islam, the best struggle is always fought on a battlefield
Abu Dawud: the best jihad is a word of justice before an unjust ruler. a sentence, not a sword.
one hadith says change a wrong with your hand, then your tongue, then at least your heart
that's the ladder in Sahih Muslim; the heart alone is the weakest of faith.
Muslim scholars all agree a correction should always be made in public
some scholars press advising those in authority privately first, citing a report in Musnad Ahmad.

games.q: at Eid lunch your aunt makes a cutting joke about your cousin, in front of everyone. you lean toward speaking up right there. what's the best case for the other side, speaking to her privately?
o: it guards her dignity and gives her room to change without losing face.
it keeps lunch comfortable, so nobody has to feel awkward at the table.
it's the only way the Qur'an allows a correction to be made at all.
games.why: the private view isn't about comfort. it protects the one corrected and gives room to change. and both views agree: silence about a real wrong isn't the middle.

practice: Bring to mind one true thing that needs saying to someone. Shape it into one short sentence with no insult in it, then say it once, quietly, out loud, just to hear it in your own voice. Let the rest of the time be quiet around it.

wordCard.voice: Speaking truth: saying what's right to the one who needs to hear it, even when it costs you. The hadith calls it the best struggle.

orig.note: Arabic: a word of truth. haqq means truth, and also a right, what is due.

carryVoice: For the road: a word of truth, said kindly, in the right room. Talk tomorrow.

sources.ref: Sunan Abu Dawud 4344 (also Jami' at-Tirmidhi 2174; Sunan an-Nasa'i 4209, 'a word of truth'): the best jihad is a word of justice before an unjust ruler
Sahih Muslim 49: whoever sees a wrong, change it with his hand, then his tongue, then his heart, the weakest of faith
Musnad Ahmad 15333 ('Iyad ibn Ghanm): whoever wants to advise a person in authority should not do it openly, but take him by the hand and do it in private
